audits.mathematicalReason: The equal angles at C and T are each (180°−36°)/2=72°. Since TR bisects the angle at T, ∠CTR=36°. With R on CA, ∠RCT=72°, so triangle CRT gives ∠CRT=180°−72°−36°=72°. Alternatively, ∠CRT is an exterior angle of triangle ART and equals 36°+36°. Both proposed routes are valid; the exterior-angle theorem is route-specific rather than universally required.

audits.mathematicalReason: Equilateral triangle ABC has all sides 4. Since D is the midpoint of AC, AD=CD=2; equilateral triangle ADE then gives DE=AE=2. Since G is the midpoint of AE, AG=GE=1; equilateral triangle EFG gives EF=FG=1. The exterior perimeter is AB+BC+CD+DE+EF+FG+GA=4+4+2+2+1+1+1=15. The equilateral-side properties and midpoint/segment calculations match the proposed scopes.

figureEvidence.fact: The exterior boundary follows A–B–C–D–E–F–G–A. D lies on AC and G lies on AE; AD and GE are shared interior segments, not exterior perimeter segments.

routes.label: Triangle sums and a linear pair

audits.mathematicalReason: In triangle AFG, the two equal angles are each (180°−20°)/2=80°. At F, ray FB agrees with FG and ray FD is opposite FA, so ∠BFD=100°. Triangle BFD consequently gives ∠B+∠D=180°−100°=80°. Equivalently, ∠AFG=80° is an exterior angle of triangle BFD and directly equals the requested sum. The listed routes correctly distinguish the linear-pair and exterior-angle alternatives.

audits.derivedAnswer: C: The product of the non-real zeros of P
audits.mathematicalReason: The graph gives real zeros 2 and β with 3<β<4, and d=P(0) lies between 4 and 6. The three visible turning points exhaust those possible for a quartic, so there are no additional real zeros. If u and v are the non-real zeros, the monic quartic root-product identity gives 2βuv=d. Hence 0<uv=d/(2β)<1. Meanwhile, the product of all zeros is d>4, the sum of the real zeros is 2+β>5, and both P(−1) and P(1) exceed 2. The coefficient sum equals P(1), so the non-real-root product is the smallest. Graph reading, root–coefficient identities, and substitution are all defensible in the proposed roles.

figureEvidence.fact: The curve crosses the x-axis at x=2 and again between 3 and 4. It shows two local minima and one local maximum, with the left minimum above the x-axis.
The y-intercept lies between 4 and 6, and the plotted values at x=−1 and x=1 are both above 2. Only these coarse bounds, not exact coefficient values, are used.

audits.mathematicalReason: Index rows from the top and columns from the left; the holes satisfy 1≤c≤r≤5. Five yellow pegs require exactly one yellow in every row and column. The single hole in row 1 forces yellow at (1,1), then row 2 forces yellow at (2,2), and so on. After removing those positions, the four reds are similarly forced at r=c+1, the three greens at r=c+2, the two blues at r=c+3, and orange at (5,1). Thus the rows are Y; R Y; G R Y; B G R Y; O B G R Y. This is one valid placement and is uniquely forced. Joining every pair of holes sharing a row or column gives precisely the stated coloring restrictions.

figureEvidence.fact: The board has five left-aligned horizontal rows containing 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 holes. The holes align in five vertical columns, so its positions form the triangular array c≤r.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let s=AB. The arc-center conditions give BA=BC and AB=AC, making ABC equilateral. The depicted minor arc BC therefore has length πs/3=12, so s=36/π. For the pictured inner circle with center O and radius r, internal tangency gives AO=BO=s−r. Thus O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB. If M is its foot on AB, tangency to AB gives OM=r and AM=s/2. Pythagoras yields (s−r)²=(s/2)²+r², hence r=3s/8. Its circumference is 2πr=3πs/4=27. The proposed assessed scopes and supporting properties fit this valid method.

figureEvidence.fact: The arcs run from A to C and from B to C above segment AB, selecting the minor arcs. The requested circle is drawn inside the region bounded by those arcs and AB, internally tangent to the two parent circles and tangent to AB from above.

audits.mathematicalReason: Continuing the displayed diamond pattern, the kth outer layer adds 4k squares. Thus figure n contains N(n)=1+4(1+2+⋯+n)=1+2n(n+1). Consequently N(100)=1+2·100·101=20201. Identifying and expressing the geometric pattern is the assessed skill. Arithmetic-series summation is a valid supporting method, though the same formula can also be obtained by a geometric decomposition.

figureEvidence.fact: The figures are centered diamonds of unit squares with central row lengths 1, 3, 5, and 7. Figure 2 has row lengths 1,3,5,3,1, and figure 3 has 1,3,5,7,5,3,1, exhibiting the successive outer layers.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let X be the rightmost vertex, L the bottom-left vertex, H the intersection marked 100°, and K the intersection marked 110°. Triangle LHX has angles 40° at L and 100° at H, so its angle at X is 40°. This is also the angle at X in triangle AXK, since the relevant rays coincide. The marked angle AKX is 110°, giving ∠A=180°−110°−40°=30°. The candidate's two triangle-angle-sum applications are sufficient; no additional angle theorem is needed for this route.

figureEvidence.fact: A, H, and the rightmost vertex X lie on the same horizontal segment. The 100° marking is the interior angle LHX, and the 40° marking is the interior angle HLX.
K lies on both the descending segment from A and segment LX. The 110° marking is between rays KA and KX, so it is the interior angle at K of triangle AXK.
